doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: State of jazz: the conference, 'jazz is dead' and changing clubs
summary: Reid rejects the 'jazz is dead' claim, noting more young people involved, and that the old pop and club networks are gone.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Let’s talk about this conference we’re at. It’s an interesting state of affairs in jazz it seems like. If you come here — I just came from this little gathering of people talking about research. And in that room there was at least four or five different accents of people. In other words it was like an international group of people. And you’ve got I don’t know how many people here, and it makes jazz look really vibrant and healthy. And then you turn around and you read the typical “jazz is dead” article or — Gary Giddins said something about how can you promote this music when it’s not on radio or TV etcetera.

Well he just doesn’t know. I don’t know why or even how or why he would even make such a statement because he obviously hasn’t been or doesn’t see the things that I see, and see what a lot of other — it’s a different time than when the music that even like what you presented with Joe Williams — that’s a different era. It was a different place. And even before that, that music was really popular. I mean the pop music of that day. We’ve lost that. I mean even Broadway, because a lot of those songs came through Broadway musicals that the jazz musicians embraced to render, aren’t even as good as they used to be. So it’s not just the jazz, it’s not in that sense, but there are more young people involved listening to this music in this country than ever before. Are they going to be professional musicians like myself or other people? Probably not. But there will be some that come through that just have to, they have to, they have no choice.
